beats.narration_en: Every day, roads catch things that are completely out of control.
A car crossing into oncoming traffic.
A twenty-ton boulder falling toward the road.
Even a jet that couldn't stop in time.
Stopping them is easy. Stopping them without hurting anyone is the hard part.
Here are seven clever ways engineers do it, and the one trick almost all of them share.
Number one: the end of a guardrail.
A plain rail end is dangerous.
Hit it head on and it doesn't give way. It spears right into the cabin.
So the end gets a steel head that slides down the rail.
Inside, it squeezes the rail flat and bends it away in a long steel ribbon.
Crushing steel takes a huge force, and that force is what slows the car.
The posts near the end snap off, so nothing snags the wheels.
Sixty to zero in about two car lengths, and the cabin is untouched.
Number two: three thin steel cables.
A car that crosses the median is headed straight into oncoming traffic.
So three steel ropes are strung tight between flimsy posts.
When a car hits them, the posts just fold over.
The cables stretch back like a slingshot, about eight feet.
That long stretch slows the car gently instead of stopping it dead.
Then the tension steers it back along the median, away from the other lanes.
It's not a wall. It's a giant steel net.
Number three: a guardrail that spins.
It's a rolling barrier made in South Korea for dangerous curves.
Hit a plain steel rail and it scrapes and drags at the car.
These rollers are barrels of tough foam on steel posts.
When a car slides into them, they spin instead of scraping.
The foam squashes to soak up the hit.
And the spinning turns part of the crash into rotation.
So the car keeps rolling forward and is steered back toward its lane.
One version passed a sixty-two mile an hour crash test for American roads.
Number four: the police spike strip.
A blowout at sixty could flip the car right over.
So every spike is a hollow steel tube with a sharp tip.
As the tire rolls across, the tubes punch into the tread.
Then they snap off the strip and stay stuck in the rubber.
Air leaks out through each tube, like breathing through a straw.
The tire goes flat in about half a minute, instead of bursting.
So the car slows down on its own, still steering straight.
Number five does the opposite of a gentle stop.
At secure gates, a steel wall can jump out of the road in about a second.
Under the road, a hinged steel plate waits inside a concrete pit.
Hydraulic pistons swing its front edge up, nearly three feet high.
A car that hits it doesn't just bounce off the steel.
Thick struts push the crash down into tons of buried concrete.
So the car stops dead, and its back end flips into the air.
Tested ones can stop a fifteen thousand pound truck going fifty.
Number six: catching a twenty-ton boulder.
Mountain roads hang steel nets on the slopes above them.
The net is woven from steel rings, like chain mail.
When a rock hits, the net doesn't try to stop it dead.
It stretches like a trampoline, more than twenty feet.
And the ropes that hold it pull through brake rings.
These steel loops shrink and bend, turning the speed into heat.
A slow stop keeps the forces low, so nothing snaps.
The biggest nets stop twenty tons at sixty miles an hour.
Afterward, crews clear the rock and replace the brakes.
And number seven: stopping a jet.
Sometimes a jet can't stop and runs off the end of the runway.
So many airports add a bed of crushable concrete blocks.
It looks like pavement, but it's light and full of bubbles.
Under the weight of a plane, the blocks crush.
The tires sink in, like driving into deep sand.
Every block they crush takes away some of the speed.
It's built to stop a jet rolling in at eighty miles an hour.
It has already stopped more than two dozen planes, with hundreds of people aboard.
Afterward, crews just replace the crushed blocks.
Did you spot the trick they almost all share?
A crash doesn't hurt because of speed. It hurts because the speed disappears too fast.
So engineers stretch the stop out.
Steel that crushes, cables that stretch, nets that give, and blocks that crumble.
The longer the stop, the smaller the force.
